name: ePTFE (Gore-Tex) facial implant
lead: Expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE), best known under the brand name Gore-Tex, is a flexible, porous synthetic material that surgeons have used to add projection or volume to the chin, lips, nasolabial folds and nasal dorsum. Placed through a small incision, the soft white implant is shaped to the patient's anatomy and then held in place as tissue grows into its pores, so the profile or facial balance changes for as long as the implant stays in. People who want a stronger chin or a higher nasal bridge without moving bone or relying on repeated filler sessions are the usual audience for synthetic implants of this kind [2][11][13].

The material was created in 1969 by Robert (Bob) Gore, who stretched heated PTFE rods rapidly rather than slowly, producing a microporous structure that is about 70% air [1]. Because it is nearly inert in the body and lets tissue grow through it, ePTFE became a standard material for vascular grafts, sutures, heart patches and synthetic ligaments long before facial surgeons adopted it [1][12]. Its use in rhinoplasty was first reported in 1989, according to a later revision-surgery study, and it has since been used as a chin, lip and cheek-region onlay as well [13].

Published cosmetic work consists mostly of surgeon case series and literature reviews: a 1997 evaluation of Gore-Tex lip augmentation [3], a rhinoplasty review noting both advocates and opponents of alloplast use [4], a 2008 meta-analysis of alloplastic nasal implants [15], and a comparison study in Asian nasal dorsal augmentation [5]. Reviews describe ePTFE as having low tissue reactivity and a long track record, while also describing infection, displacement and difficult removal as its main trade-offs [13][14]. Patients' own cartilage remains the material many surgeons prefer for the nose [14][16][17].

paras: Expanded PTFE is chemically inert, thermally stable and has tunable porosity; in the Gore-Tex membrane form it is about 70% air [1]. A 2008 overview of nasal dorsal augmentation describes it as a carbon-fluorine polymer of solid nodes joined by fine fibrils, with low tissue reactivity, a hydrophobic surface that discourages bacterial adherence, and a microporous structure whose tissue ingrowth stabilises the implant. The same overview notes that it does not resorb, though it may slowly change shape or develop palpable edges, and that its whitish colour can show through thin skin [14].

For facial work the material is supplied as sheets or blocks of different thicknesses. Sheets work as fill or contour grafts and offer little structural support on their own, while the firmer block form has been used less often [14]. A revision-surgery study puts the pore size at about 10 to 30 micrometres, large enough for fibroblasts and connective tissue to enter [13]. Surgeons describe it as easy to carve or layer, though it is slippery and can shift in the early post-operative period before ingrowth anchors it [14].

In the body ePTFE is used in vascular grafts, sutures, heart patches, synthetic ligaments and glaucoma surgery membranes [1]. The lip-implant variants developed from the same membrane technology are covered under Lip implants below [11].

Facial implants of this kind are used to change the outline of a region from the outside, by pushing overlying soft tissue outward over a flat or recessed area, which adds convexity and projection [11].

In chin augmentation, ePTFE is described as flexible, strong and porous, fixed to bone with titanium screws, with tissue ingrowth providing most of the hold [2]. A 2000 review of chin augmentation lists Gore-Tex alongside Medpor, Supramid, Silastic and Mersilene among alloplastic chin implants, and concludes that no single implant suits every face [19]. The aim described is a projection and height in balance with the other features, often combined with rhinoplasty. Chin implant surgery can improve the chin's appearance but does not correct dental occlusion, which requires mandibular surgery [2].

The nasal dorsum, tip and columella are the other main targets. A 1995 review of nasal implants judged Gore-Tex to be gaining in popularity, citing animal studies of its biocompatibility, while still giving autogenous tissue as the authors' preferred method of augmenting the dorsum [18]. The 2003 Facial Plastic Surgery review describes the material as attracting attention over about 30 years from both advocates and opponents, with surgeon hesitation grounded in the history of earlier nasal implants [4]. A 2010 paper asked whether ePTFE is an alternative for nasal dorsal augmentation in Asian patients [5]. Wikipedia's rhinoplasty article states that autologous cartilage and bone are generally preferred to prostheses for the dorsum because of lower rejection and complication rates, with a synthetic graft used when no autologous graft is available [16]. A facial-feminisation surgery group reported in JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery that it never uses silicone, ePTFE or high-density polyethylene in rhinoplasty, citing long-term complications such as infection, displacement and protrusion [17].

A 1997 study in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery evaluated lip augmentation with a Gore-Tex facial implant [3]. A 2009 soft-tissue augmentation review reports that earlier tubular ePTFE lip implants performed poorly in some patients because of complete tissue ingrowth and hardening, that later designs were better tolerated though judged not to match the softness of hyaluronic acid gel, and that a newer saline-filled implant uses an inner elastic membrane and an outer microscopic ePTFE membrane separated by a slip plane to mimic lip tissue [11].

For the chin, Wikipedia's overview lists silicone, porous polyethylene (Medpor) and ePTFE as the main synthetic options. Silicone is smooth and does not bond to tissue, so the pocket has to be precise, and it is relatively easy to remove. Porous polyethylene is firmer and tissue grows into it, which anchors it but makes removal harder. ePTFE is flexible, soft and strong, and its porosity lets soft tissue and bone growth hold it in place [2].

The 2008 nasal overview describes ePTFE as perhaps the most reliable solid implant material available through 2006, and contrasts the main limitation of each material: infection for ePTFE, extrusion for silicone (complication rates of 4 to 36% in Western series), resorption for Supramid and fragmentation for Proplast. It calls Medpor more rigid and says autologous cartilage remains the gold standard, with alloplastic materials generally reserved for patients with insufficient autologous tissue [14]. A 1995 review similarly said silicone had fallen out of favour because of bad publicity and concern about autoimmune disease, and that Medpor never enjoyed wide use over the dorsum because of its rigidity [18].

Chin implants are placed in a pocket reached through an incision under the chin or inside the lower lip. Some are fixed to the mandible and others are held only by the pocket [2]. The review of skeletal onlay grafts describes insertion through an incision with dissection above or below the periosteum, followed by bone fixation or suture techniques, and notes that choosing the right implant size is the main practical challenge, one reason computer-aided design and trial sizers are used [11].
A sliding genioplasty, which moves a piece of the patient's own jaw bone forward, is the alternative that adds no foreign material [2].

Polytetrafluoroethylene itself was discovered by Roy Plunkett at DuPont in 1938 [12]. Wikipedia's Gore-Tex article records that John Cropper of New Zealand made stretched PTFE tape in 1966 but kept the method secret, and that Bob Gore, son of W. L. Gore, stretched heated rods rapidly in 1969 so that they expanded about 800% into ePTFE, which the company sold under the Gore-Tex trademark [1].

Gore obtained a US patent in 1976 and in 1983 the Federal Circuit recognised the company as the inventor of ePTFE in W. L. Gore v. Garlock. The main claim of the product patent was later declared invalid in 1990, and the company's ePTFE patents expired in 1997 [1]. Robert Gore was inducted into the US National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2006 [1].

In rhinoplasty, a 2014 study of revision cases dates first use to 1989 by Rothstein and Jacob [13]. Large series followed, including a multicentre review of 309 patients [14], and a 2001 retrospective study of 66 patients reported use for nasal dorsum augmentation [1]. The 2008 overview of nasal dorsal augmentation noted that the manufacturer had recently discontinued production of the material for plastic-surgery applications [14].

A 2008 meta-analysis in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery searched MEDLINE from 1966 to 2005 and compared the three most widely used nasal alloplasts; it reported a removal rate of 3.1% for both Gore-Tex and Medpor and a significantly higher 6.5% for silicone [15].

The 2008 overview cites a 309-patient multicentre study with a mean follow-up of 40.4 months in which no grafts displaced or resorbed and ten patients (3.2%) had infections requiring removal; the only predisposing factor identified was a preoperative septal perforation [14]. The 2014 revision study cites other series reporting complication or infection rates of roughly 2.5% to 4% for ePTFE, and one comparison reporting 4.11% for ePTFE used as a dorsal onlay against 21.24% for porous polyethylene used as a columellar strut [13].

The same 2014 paper is a retrospective review of 581 revisional rhinoplasties in which 183 involved Gore-Tex, 376 silicone and 22 Medpor. In the Gore-Tex group the problems recorded were infection (44 cases), displacement (11), tip problems (97) and dorsal problems (31), and none were recorded as protrusion. The authors note that the figures come from a revision population and that the study is retrospective; they recommend choosing implants by material properties and conclude without singling out one material. They also cite critics who point to weakness under physical shock, unconfirmed fibrovascular ingrowth, difficult removal and volume reduction [13].

The 2009 review reports that patients should expect swelling and temporary numbness for roughly three weeks, with the surrounding capsule maturing after about six months. Its author reports no clinically significant bone or soft-tissue loss from skeletal onlay implants of this type, citing about 30 years of widespread use, and describes them as reversible if removal is required [11].

Tissue ingrowth is both the attraction and the trade-off. Ingrowth stabilises the implant, and the 2008 nasal overview says it adheres firmly enough to resist migration while still being removable if needed [14]. The 2014 revision study describes one patient in whom ingrowth after dorsal augmentation made the implant difficult to remove cleanly [13]. Published reports are largely surgeon case series, and the rhinoplasty literature notes that large series with long-term follow-up are still wanted [4].

Studies of cosmetic ePTFE are surgeon case series, retrospective reviews and one meta-analysis. A 1997 study evaluated lip augmentation with Gore-Tex [3]; a literature review covers ePTFE in rhinoplasty, including techniques and outcomes [4]; a meta-analysis of nasal alloplasts reported removal rates by material [15]; a retrospective review of 581 revision rhinoplasties tallied complications by implant type [13]; and a 2010 paper addresses nasal dorsal augmentation in Asian patients [5].

Most other published ePTFE studies concern non-cosmetic uses, such as laryngeal vocal fold medialisation [7][8] and glaucoma surgery, including a randomised trial of mitomycin-C [9]. A registered trial of Gore-Tex implants for atrophic rhinitis was suspended with five participants [10]. These do not examine appearance outcomes.

Common effects after chin implant surgery are swelling, hematoma and lower-lip weakness or numbness that usually resolves. Less common are infection, bony changes, displacement of the implant and nerve damage, and surgeon experience is described as reducing the chance of complications [2]. Because tissue grows into porous ePTFE, removal is described as more involved than with smooth silicone [2].

For the nose, the literature names infection, early displacement and, in revision series, contour problems at the tip and dorsum as the main concerns; delayed infection or immune reactivity is associated with the roughly 3% short-term extrusion rate cited in one overview [13][14]. The facial-feminisation group quoted above lists infections, implant displacement and protrusions among the long-term complications they associate with alloplastic nasal materials [17]. Surgeons' reluctance about alloplasts in the nose is attributed in the literature to the history of earlier nasal implants [4].

Implants for the chin and jaw are discussed in hardmaxxing contexts as a way to raise chin projection without cutting bone. ePTFE comes up as one of several materials alongside silicone and porous polyethylene, with discussion centred on material choice, tissue ingrowth and removal. The material is also familiar to the public through its outdoor-apparel membrane, which belongs to the same fluoropolymer family as the surgical products [1][12].

lore.intro: Discussion of ePTFE facial implants takes place mostly in the surgical literature, where advocates and critics of alloplastic materials are named in reviews, and in hardmaxxing threads on chin and jaw implants, where it is mentioned beside silicone and Medpor.[4][2]

claims.claim: ePTFE is a reliable, well-tolerated alternative to silicone and Medpor
claims.believers: Advocates cite its low tissue reactivity, biocompatibility, easy shaping and low infection and removal rates in large series.[14][15]
claims.experts: A 2008 meta-analysis found a 3.1% removal rate for Gore-Tex against 6.5% for silicone, though the abstract does not report infection or extrusion rates.[15] Reviewers say large long-term series are still wanted.[4]

claims.claim: Tissue ingrowth holds the implant securely in place
claims.believers: Proponents say ingrowth anchors the implant and resists migration while still allowing removal.[2][14]
claims.experts: The 2008 overview says it can still shift early before ingrowth, and critics cited in a 2014 study question whether fibrovascular ingrowth is confirmed.[13][14]

claims.believers: Some patients and surgeons describe porous implants as harder to take out than smooth silicone.[2]
claims.experts: A 2014 revision series described one case in which an ingrown dorsal implant was hard to remove cleanly; the 2008 overview describes ePTFE as removable if needed.[13][14]

claims.claim: Synthetic nasal implants carry long-term risk compared with patient's own cartilage
claims.believers: Surgeons who avoid alloplasts cite infection, displacement and protrusion and prefer septal, ear or rib cartilage.[17]
claims.experts: Wikipedia's rhinoplasty article states autologous grafts are preferred for lower rejection and complication rates, and the 2008 overview calls autologous cartilage the gold standard.[14][16]

claims.claim: ePTFE lip implants give natural-feeling fullness
claims.believers: A 1997 study evaluated Gore-Tex lip augmentation as a surgical option for fuller lips.[3][3]
claims.experts: A 2009 review reports that earlier tubular implants hardened because of ingrowth and that later designs did not match hyaluronic acid softness.[11]

claims.claim: The material is no longer widely available for cosmetic surgery
claims.believers: Hardmaxxing discussion treats it as one option among chin and nose implant materials.[2]
claims.experts: A 2008 overview reports that the manufacturer had recently discontinued production of the material for plastic-surgery applications.[14]

card.summary: Gore-Tex-type porous synthetic implant used for chin, lip, nasolabial and nasal augmentation; cosmetic studies are small and mostly older.
card.note: Porous material that tissue grows into; cosmetic evidence limited to small series and reviews.

quick.overview:
Expanded PTFE, sold as Gore-Tex, is a flexible porous synthetic used in implants for the chin, lips, nasolabial folds and nose. It was developed in 1969 and is widely used elsewhere in medicine, for example in grafts and sutures.

Cosmetic evidence in the reviewed material is limited to a lip-augmentation study, a rhinoplasty literature review and an Asian nasal dorsum study.
quick.mechanism: The microporous material is shaped and placed in a pocket, in the chin attached to bone with titanium screws, and tissue grows into its pores to help hold it [2].
quick.risks: General implant risks include swelling, infection, displacement and nerve injury. Surgeons quoted in the rhinoplasty review express hesitation about alloplast use because of historical experience with earlier nasal implants [4].

chain: A soft, porous ePTFE piece is placed through a small incision
Tissue grows into the implant and holds it in position
Chin projection, lip fullness or nasal dorsum height is increased
angle.text: ePTFE implants add volume or projection to the chin, lips, nasolabial folds or nasal dorsum, so the profile and facial balance change. The effect is surgical and lasting, with the implant held by tissue ingrowth and, for chin pieces, titanium screws.
